Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for South Africa's reply. As per Natalie Germanos on air, Melie Kerr has not taken the field just yet. Whether it is due to the fatigue of her knock or any other issue, remains to be seen. Hannah Rowe has come on as a substitute for Kerr. It will be Laura Wolvaardt and Tazmin Brits to open the innings for South Africa. Rosemary Mair will start with the new ball for New Zealand. Away we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, New Zealand Women will be the happier of the two sides at the halfway mark. No side has ever successfully chased a 150-plus score in the final of the Women's T20 World Cup, highlighting the monumental task that lies ahead for South Africa. The wicket is on the drier side with the balls gripping in the surface for the slower bowlers but as has been the trend this tournament in Dubai, the ball comes onto the bat nicely under lights. Will that be the case tonight as well? It remains to be seen. A good Powerplay will put South Africa in good stead for the rest of the chase while New Zealand will look to take this momentum into their bowling effort. Back in a bit for the chase.

Brooke Halliday is in for a chat. She says it was good to bat with Melie Kerr and also says it was good to bat with such a good crowd. Tells they batted well but also mentions that the wicket was a bit sticky and slow in nature. Adds they wanted to be proactive and keep rotating the strike. Also adds that it was getting lower and slower and thinks their spinners will come into play. Is hopeful that they will defend this total.

Once the field restrictions were lifted, South Africa managed to tighten the screws with their spinners and Nadine De Klerk leading the charge. During that middle phase, the White Ferns found it difficult to score freely, going a staggering 49 balls without hitting a boundary. Melie Kerr struggled to break free under pressure, but then Brooke Halliday stepped up to take the pressure off her.  Halliday's 38 off 28 set the White Ferns up nicely for the back end of their innings. Kerr's couple of lusty blows towards the end and Maddy Green's 12 off 6 propelled them to 158.

New Zealand Women finish on a high! They will take this total on any day of the week, especially on the night of the final. After struggling to get out of the rut in the middle phase, they managed to regain the lost ground. The White Ferns managed 73 runs in the last 6 overs to end up with 158 on the board. Earlier in the innings, after being put into bat, Georgia Plimmer made her intentions clear right from the start with a couple of boundaries in the first over. Although she couldn't kick on, Suzie Bates maintained the tempo during the Powerplay.

IN THE AIR AND DROPPED! It swirls over the long on region where Sune Luus scoots to her left and settles well underneath it but eventually puts it down and allows two runs to be taken.

Commentary.Commentary: Drinks break! This has been a cagey start to the final. The White Ferns, having lost Suzie Bates are in a rebuilding phase. South Africa will look to apply the squeeze here, with Sophie Devine still relatively new at the crease and Melie Kerr yet to fully come to terms with the surface. The ball has been holding on the surface and therefore, New Zealand will need to carefully assess their target on this pitch and avoid aiming too high while South Africa who have already given away 9 runs in extras, will have to tighten up in that aspect. A change in bowling as well, Nadine De Klerk replaces Marizanne Kapp.

OUT! BOWLED'EM! Excellent pace variation at display! Nonkululeko Mlaba strikes and provides a very crucial breakthrough for the Proteas Women! Commentary.Commentary: Done and dusted with the pre-match formalities as 'God Defend New Zealand' and 'Nkosi Sikelel Afrika' are proudly sung by the respective players of both nations. It is now time for the action to get underway at the DICS! It is a FULL HOUSE in Dubai as the two umpires walk out to the middle. The players of South Africa Women scatter out in the field after a long discussion in the team huddle near the ropes. Out walk the two openers of New Zealand Women - Suzie Bates, representing New Zealand in her 334th international game. She will be partnered by the young Georgia Plimmer. And it will be Marizanne Kapp to kick off the proceedings of the Grand Finale. And, here we go...

The flags of the two nations unfurl at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium. And now, the two set of players follow the match officials and line up for their respective national anthems. It will be New Zealand's first, followed by the national anthem of South Africa.

Just a few moments before the start of the finale then. But before that, the ICC Hall of Fame inductees, Sir Alastair Cook and Neetu David walk out on the carpet with the glittering silverware and place it on the pedestal for the photo-ops.

PITCH REPORT - Mpumelelo Mbangwa gives us a lowdown on the conditions ahead of the final. He notes that the noise around the stadium is starting to build, and it's not too muggy tonight. Mbangwa points out that we're positioned in the centre, with the square boundaries measuring 61 and 60 meters, while the straight hit will be longer - 73 meters. Lisa Sthalekar joins him and says she isn’t surprised by South Africa’s decision to bowl first. Adds that the wicket looks to be on the drier side. She explains that the ball tends to come onto the bat quicker under the lights here in Dubai, which will benefit batters later on. Sthalekar reckons that New Zealand must keep that in mind and go hard with the bat. She also mentions that the average score is 127, but considering it’s the final, a target around 140 could be very competitive.

The captain of New Zealand Women, Sophie Devine says they would have batted first so it has worked well for both teams. Thinks this looks like a good surface and they want to put good runs on the board. Adds that it is not just another game, it is more important than every other game. Is delighted to see the crowd and they are just trying to soak it all in. Informs they are going with the same side. Is also delighted to see the men's team doing exceptionally well in India, winning a Test after a long while. Ends by saying they certainly take inspiration from them and from what they are capable to do.

The captain of South Africa, Laura Wolvaardt says that bowling first has worked really well for them throughout the tournament and they want to stick to that. Feels that it is massive for them as a team to be in this position and need to work really hard here to get the result. Informs that they are going unchanged for this game.

South Africa Women (Playing XI) - Laura Wolvaardt (C), Tazmin Brits, Anneke Bosch, Marizanne Kapp, Sune Luus, Chloe Tryon, Nadine De Klerk, Annerie Dercksen, Sinalo Jafta (WK), Nonkululeko Mlaba, Ayabonga Khaka.
New Zealand Women (Playing XI) - Suzie Bates, Georgia Plimmer, Melie Kerr, Sophie Devine (C), Brooke Halliday, Maddy Green, Izzy Gaze (WK), Rosemary Mair, Lea Tahuhu, Eden Carson, Fran Jonas.
TOSS UPDATE - The flip of the coin lands in the favour of South Africa Women and Laura Wolvaardt elects to BOWL first.

In Women's T20Is, New Zealand hold a significant advantage, having secured 11 victories compared to South Africa's 4 wins in their previous encounters. However, past records hold little weight in a final, where the stakes are high and anything can happen. It all comes down to who performs better on the night. This showdown promises to be a classic, with the title up for grabs and glory just 40 overs away. Who will reign supreme? Join us for this exhilarating ride to find out!

On the other hand, New Zealand are in a Women's T20 World Cup final for the first time in 14 years. Coming into the tournament on the back of a 10-game losing streak in the format, few expected them to make such a deep run. However, since their dominant victory over India in the campaign opener, the White Ferns have defied the odds and built significant momentum. Led by Sophie Devine, they have turned the tables and now stand on the brink of a historic triumph, with a chance to claim their first-ever Women's T20 World Cup title.

After stumbling at the final hurdle in 2023, South Africa find themselves once again within touching distance of glory. Laura Wolvaardt and Co. are eager to exorcise the ghosts of that Cape Town heartbreak and finally end South Africa's long wait for an ICC trophy in senior cricket across genders. Their confidence is soaring, especially after humbling the World Cup behemoth, Australia, in the semifinal. Earlier this year, the men came agonizingly close but fell short in the final against India and now the 'Rainbow Nation' anxiously awaits a different outcome, hoping their women can deliver the elusive title.

The day of reckoning is here! It's time for the summit clash of the 2024 ICC Women's T20 World Cup. What began as a fierce competition among 10 teams has now culminated in a thrilling climax. After weeks of breathtaking cricket, 8 teams have bowed out, leaving just two standing - South Africa and New Zealand - both poised to achieve cricketing immortality. By the end of today, a new champion will rise, forever etched in the annals of ICC Women's T20 World Cup history. Hello and welcome from the Dubai International Cricket Stadium, gleaming under the lights and ready to host this epic final.
... MATCH DAY ...

The wait is over and the Grand Finale of the ICC Women's T20 World Cup, 2024 is here! After almost three weeks of high-octane cricketing action, we have finally reached the summit clash where South Africa Women will be taking on New Zealand Women at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium in Dubai, UAE. It has been a long and hard-fought road for both these sides who are looking to lift the coveted T20 World Cup trophy for the very first time which guarantees us a new champion. Neither side was really touted as the favorites to win it all at the start of the tournament but both these sides have shown great character in order to breach barriers and put themselves in one of the biggest clashes of their cricketing careers. Let's now talk about the form and journeys of both sides starting with South Africa Women. The Proteas came into the tournament filled with expectations of repeating their showing in the previous T20 World Cup at home but there were certain doubts as well. Thankfully, they managed to stitch together an experienced side with quite a few players recovering from injuries. Skipper Laura Wolvaardt has led the team brilliantly so far whilst keeping her own form with the bat going. They started their journey with a demolition job of West Indies which gave them great confidence but were beaten in the next game by England. With two difficult games out of the way, the Proteas needed to win the next two games and they did so quite comprehensively against Scotland and Bangladesh. Laura Wolvaardt and Tazmin Brits have been the standout opening pair and currently are the top two run-getters of the tournament as well and their exploits in the Powerplay could be vital in the Final. Nonkululeko Mlaba has notched up 10 wickets, second only to Melie Kerr whereas Marizanne Kapp has yet again proved her worth with both bat and ball when needed. Also, given how Anneke Bosch played in that semi-final, South Africa Women will feel much more positively about that middle order if the openers are unable to get the job done. Moving on to New Zealand Women, they were completely out of form in 2024 and were on a string of losses heading into the main event. But they managed to pull off a huge win against India in their opening clash and that made all the difference in the world. They were humbled by rivals Australia once again but managed to beat another in-form side in Sri Lanka and then in the last group stage game, they ran riot against Pakistan with the ball, sealing a semi-final berth. In the repeat of the 2016 semi-final, the White Ferns managed to exorcise their demons and beat West Indies by 8 runs in a thrilling contest to enter their first T20 World Cup Final since 2010. Just like their opponents, the opening partnership will be crucial for the Kiwis and one of Suzie Bates or Georgia Plimmer will have to play a starring role. They do have pinch-hitters at the death and the duo of Sophie Devine and Melie Kerr in the middle order can turn things around as well. Kerr has been prolific with the ball and is the highest wicket-taker of the tournament with 12 wickets to her name and would want to contribute with the bat as well if need be. New Zealand Women have lifted a major ICC trophy and would love to get their hands on the T20 World Cup trophy but if South Africa Women were to win, they would make history as the first side, men or women to win an ICC World Cup. Proteas men came so close just a few months ago in the Caribbean, can the women do one better? Or will the White Ferns write their name in the history books after a long wait? Only time will tell.
